# Atmospheric steam engine (Newcomen type) (`atmospheric_engine`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: needs atmospheric_pressure, piston_pump, safety_valve_boiler; helped by boring_machine, sand_loam_casting, savery_steam_pump, coal_mining
- Core idea: Atmospheric pressure drives the working stroke. Condensing steam lowers the pressure beneath the piston, and the boiler supplies the energy for the cycle. A vertical cylinder, open at the top, stands on a low-pressure boiler. Its piston hangs by a chain from one end of a rocking beam; the heavy pump rods hang from the other end and pull the piston up, drawing in steam at barely more than atmospheric pressure. Then the steam valve shuts and a jet of cold water is sprayed inside the cylinder: the steam condenses, leaving a partial vacuum, and the air pressing on top of the piston (at most 101 kPa at sea level, or about 22 kN on a 53 cm piston; residual vapour, air and friction reduce the useful force) drives it down and lifts the pump rods. Parts: boiler with safety valve, cylinder (cast brass, later iron), piston packed with leather or hemp and sealed by a layer of water on top, steam valve, injection cock fed from a cistern above, a drain pipe with one-way valve for the condensate, a snifting valve to blow out air, and a plug rod on the beam that works the valves. The mine pump also needs its own barrel and check valves. A note on an early drawing reports twelve strokes per minute, each lifting ten gallons through 51 yards.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking steam pushes the piston; raising the pressure adds nothing here and endangers the boiler
  - Cooling the cylinder only from outside; it is far too slow. Injecting water inside was the decisive step
  - No snifting valve: air from the feed and injection water collects and destroys the vacuum within a few strokes
  - Relying on a tight piston fit; the cylinder could not be made truly round, so the water seal on top is essential
  - Expecting economy; it turns under 1 % of the coal's heat into work and pays only where coal is nearly free
- History: europe: 1654 – Guericke shows the force of air on a piston; 1673 Huygens's gunpowder cylinder; 1690 Papin's model: steam condensed under a piston; 1712 Thomas Newcomen and John Calley's engine near Dudley Castle, built under Savery's patent; iron cylinders from Coalbrookdale in the 1720s; 1770s Smeaton doubles the efficiency. Whether Newcomen knew Papin's work is not known; americas: 1753–1755 – first engine in North America, Schuyler copper mine, New Jersey
- Read:
  - Mårten Triewald, Short Description of the Atmospheric Engine (1734; English tr. Newcomen Society, 1928)
  - L. T. C. Rolt & J. S. Allen, The Steam Engine of Thomas Newcomen (1977)
  - H. W. Dickinson, A Short History of the Steam Engine (1939)
